title: Growing dill microgreens
subtitle: Fine feathery herb microgreens with a concentrated dill flavour, cut in 10 to 14 days
excerpt: Dill microgreens are fine, feathery herb cotyledons with a concentrated dill flavour. They take 10 to 14 days on a 25 cm indoor tray and are most useful as a garnish or flavouring for fish dishes, cucumber salads, and eggs.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Dill microgreens are a year-round indoor tray crop with a 10 to 14 day cycle. Sow on a pre-dampened seed compost tray, blackout for two to three days, then grow in bright light until the feathery cotyledons are 5 to 8 cm tall. The flavour is more concentrated than mature dill because the aromatic oils are undiluted in the small seedling.
Dill microgreens are most useful as a finishing garnish or flavouring; the feathery texture means they break down under heat. Use fresh.

Light: a bright south-facing windowsill in spring and summer. A grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray at 14 to 16 hours per day is recommended in winter. Dill microgreens in low light become leggy and pale, and the flavour becomes weaker.
Temperature: 16 to 22°C. Dill microgreens are tolerant of a moderate temperature range; they perform adequately at 15°C but do best in the 18 to 22°C range.

Day 0: sow. Fill the tray with pre-dampened seed compost to within 1 cm of the rim. Dill seed is flat and oval. Scatter at 15 to 20 g per 25 cm tray, distributing evenly. Press gently into contact with the medium but do not bury; dill seed germinates at or just below the surface.
Days 1 to 3: blackout. Cover with a second tray, lightly weighted. Dill germinates in two to three days; remove the cover when the majority of shoots are upright at 2 to 3 cm.
Day 4 onward: light. The feathery cotyledons open and green up within 24 hours of moving to a bright position.
daily: set the growing tray inside a second tray with 1 to 2 cm of water. Remove excess after 30 minutes.

Days 10 to 14: cut. When the feathery cotyledons are fully open and 5 to 8 cm tall, cut 1 cm above the medium surface. Rinse gently under cold water and use fresh. Dill microgreens wilt quickly after cutting.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems on dill microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Uneven germination with many gaps in coverage
items.cause: Uneven sowing density or low seed viability.
items.fix: Scatter seed more systematically on the next attempt: work in rows across the tray. Use fresh seed; dill seed has a shorter viable window than brassica seed.

items.symptom: Cotyledons pale and weak after moving to light
items.cause: Insufficient light or removed from blackout too early.
items.fix: Move to a brighter position or add a grow light. Remove the blackout cover only once shoots are at least 2 cm tall.
Bottom-water only. Ensure the room has adequate airflow.

content.text: Use untreated dill seed. Dill seed sold for culinary use (dried dill seed in spice jars) is usually steam-treated and will not germinate. Buy from a vegetable seed supplier or a microgreen seed supplier. Dill seed viability declines after 1 to 2 years; use fresh seed each season.
risk is low if bottom-watered and grown in a well-ventilated space. Dill microgreens are moderately robust compared to basil.
